# Home office deduction

I work from the box room (2.4 m × 2.9 m) at the back of the semi in Meanwood. Two ways to claim it as a sole trader, and I flip-flop every year, so here's the comparison for good.

## Option 1: simplified flat rate

HMRC monthly amounts, based on hours worked at home:

- 25 to 50 hours: £10
- 51 to 100 hours: £18
- 101+ hours: £26

I log about 120 hours a month in Toggl, so £26 × 12 = **£312 a year**. No receipts, no arguments.

## Option 2: actual costs, apportioned

7 rooms (kitchen and bathroom excluded by my own rule, so 5 counted), 1 used as the office: 1/5. Then by time: the room is used for work about 50 of 168 hours a week, roughly 30%. So 6% of the bills.

2023/24 figures:

| Bill | Annual | 6% |
|---|---|---|
| Energy (Octopus) | £2,104 | £126.24 |
| Council tax | £1,961 | £117.66 |
| Mortgage interest only | £8,640 | £518.40 |
| Water | £540 | £32.40 |

Total: £794.70. Plus broadband business share 50% of £38 × 12 = £228 (that's claimable separately under either method).

## Why I still use the flat rate

The £482 extra from option 2 saves £193 in tax at 40%. Against that:

- Claiming mortgage interest on part of a main residence makes some people nervous about Private Residence Relief when selling. As long as the room isn't **exclusively** for business (the kids do homework in there, Theo's Lego lives on the shelf) there's no CGT problem. Still.
- More to justify if HMRC ever asks.

Decision 2023/24: flat rate + broadband. Revisit if the smart heating data from [[Smart thermostat install]] shows the office zone is a bigger share of the gas than I think. Entered on [[Self assessment 2024]].

## The German comparison

For comparison, the German rules are completely different (daily flat rate, cap of €1,260). Notes from helping Javier's sister Lucía in Köln: [[Steuererklärung Homeoffice]].
